newsitem.title: PERU: MINING - Peru's sales program set for biggest test.
newsitem.headline: MINING - Peru's sales program set for biggest test.

text.p: Peru's state miner Centromin is readying for the most important sale in its ongoing, and so far, successsful series of privatizations with plans to sell in March the huge, outdated La Oroya complex, analysts said.
"La Oroya is going to be the most important sale. It's a very big asset," Guillermo Arbe, head of Peru research at Morgan Grenfell in Lima, said.
"It is viewed as a special case," because La Oroya, being an asset that processes rather than mines mineral, is the only metallurgic unit on Centromin's sell-off slate, Arbe added.

The La Oroya complex of smelters and refineries, which lies in the country's central Andes 12,300 feet (3,700 meters) above sea level and 120 miles (190 km) east of Lima, processes 22 different metals and sub-products.
The market has already forced two delays to the sale of the complex, which was first built in 1921, due to severe environmental liabilities.
But now two "major" companies were "very seriously" interested in the sale and many others were showing enthusiasm, Centromin spokesman, Enrique Olivares, said.

Industry sources said the government seemed to have found at least one sure buyer in Mexico's Penoles but needed to drum up more interest to provide competition at the auction, provisionally planned for late March.

"The general feeling among companies has been a concern over the environmental issue, but Centromin has worked hard to improve the situation," Josilu Carbonel, mining analyst at Santander Investment in Lima, said.
"It depends on how they can make it attractive through the terms of the sale."

Centromin is working on a scheme for the sell-off where the new La Oroya owner would become the majority shareholder of a mixed company formed with the government. The buyer would then gradually receive a larger stake as it injected capital, offered at the sale, to modernize the complex.

The scheme would be attractive because, first, it would mean an insignificant purchase price and, second, the buyer would "feel secure that the government was continuing to work to improve La Oroya," said Olivares.

The buyer could also be "calm" about demands to improve La Oroya's environmental record because Peruvian law allows a ten year period for refineries and smelters to "implement the appropriate modifications," he added.

Moreover, the government has also persuaded the local municipality to take responsibility for supplying drinking water to the town's population of 60,000, a task previously assigned to the La Oroya owner, and is rehousing 800 of the complex's 3,000 workers further from its toxic gas emissions.
It is this kind of flexibility and pre-planning that has been the key to making Centromin's investor-friendly privatization program a succcess, analysts said.
The 1994 attempt to sell Centromin as a whole failed to attract a single bidder.

But this year, Centromin's relaunched, piecemeal privatization has yielded rewards far exceeding expectations, attracting the world's largest mining companies to pay hundreds of millions of dollars and make investment commitments worth billions.
"It has been successful, at times spectacular," Carbonel said.

The state miner registered another big sale last week when it received a commitment from Brazil's Paranapanema to invest $100 million over five years in its polymetallic mine Yauliyacu in addition to a one-off purchase payment of $12.7 million mine.

Centromin, however, plans a slight pause in its privatizations at the beginning of next year to allow the other state miner, Minero Peru, to kick-start the second phase of its own program. Minero Peru has slated for February the auction of the Bayovar phosphate deposit that has already attracted 25 interested mining firms, according to the government.
-- Saul Hudson, Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134
